Apply a Robust Transformation to New Data, or Back-Transform

Source: R/robust_transformation.R
predict.specproc_transformation.Rd

Transforms new data with the \(\lambda\) (and, with standardize = TRUE, the mean and standard deviation of the inliers) estimated by robust_boxcox() or robust_yeojohnson(). With inverse = TRUE, it transforms values back to the original scale, such as the predictions of a model fitted to the transformed variables.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'specproc_transformation'
predict(
  object,
  newdata,
  inverse = FALSE,
  estimate = c("median", "mean"),
  residuals = NULL,
  ...
)

Arguments

object

An object returned by robust_boxcox() or robust_yeojohnson().

newdata

A numeric vector, matrix or data frame with some or all of the variables of the fit: new data, or with inverse = TRUE, values on the transformed scale.

inverse

A logical value: transform the values back to the original scale (TRUE), or transform new data (FALSE, default).

estimate

With inverse = TRUE, the estimate on the original scale: "median" (default) or "mean", which needs residuals.

residuals

With estimate = "mean", the residuals of the model on the transformed scale: a numeric vector, used for every variable of newdata, or a matrix or data frame with a column for each of them, matched by name (without column names, in the order of the columns of newdata). Missing values are ignored.

...

Not used.

Value

A tibble with the variables of newdata, in the order of the fit. Missing values stay missing, and with the Box-Cox transformation, new values that are zero or negative become NA.

Details

newdata can hold any of the variables of the fit, matched by name. A matrix or vector without column names must have all of them, in their order.

The back-transformation undoes, in reverse order, the standardization, the transformation and the pre-standardization of each variable. When a model predicts \(\hat{z}\) on the transformed scale with symmetric errors, the back-transformed value \(g^{-1}(\hat{z})\) estimates the median of the variable on the original scale (estimate = "median", the default). It needs no other assumption, and suits the prediction of one sample.

On the original scale, the mean is higher than the median when \(\lambda < 1\) (the transformation compresses the upper tail), and lower when \(\lambda > 1\). estimate = "mean" gives the smearing estimate of Duan (1983), $$\hat{x} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^{n} g^{-1}(\hat{z} + e_k),$$ where \(e_1, \dots, e_n\) are the residuals of the model on the transformed scale (preferably cross-validated, since the residuals of the fit underestimate the errors of prediction). It assumes no distribution of the errors, only that they do not depend on \(\hat{z}\). The mean matters when the predictions are averaged or summed, such as for the mean content of a lot or a mass balance. It is not robust: an outlying residual pulls it, so pass the residuals of the inliers of a robust model (for example, of the spectra that rsimpls() does not flag).

The back-transformation is not defined everywhere, because some transformations are bounded: the Box-Cox transformation above for \(\lambda < 0\), and the Yeo-Johnson transformation above for \(\lambda < 0\) and below for \(\lambda > 2\). Values beyond the bound (with estimate = "mean", values that pass it with one of the residuals) become NA, with a warning.

References

  • Duan, N. (1983). Smearing estimate: a nonparametric retransformation method. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 78(383):605-610.

See also

robust_boxcox(), robust_yeojohnson()

Examples

data(forageLIBS)
contents <- forageLIBS[c("Ca", "K", "P", "Mn")]
fit <- robust_boxcox(contents[1:300, ])
new <- predict(fit, contents[301:368, ])
# back to mg/kg
head(predict(fit, new, inverse = TRUE))
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>      Ca     K     P    Mn
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 0.431  2.25 0.229  56  
#> 2 0.805  1.91 0.21  112  
#> 3 0.786  2.61 0.312  35.0
#> 4 0.807  2.11 0.232  41  
#> 5 0.919  2.17 0.235 136  
#> 6 0.323  1.61 0.206  49  
# Box-Cox is not defined for zero or negative values
x <- contents[301:302, ]
x$Ca[2] <- 0
predict(fit, x)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>      Ca      K      P    Mn
#>   <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 -1.35  0.546 -0.400 0.465
#> 2 NA    -0.139 -0.779 2.27 

# a calibration of the transformed Mn contents on the Mn II line at
# 257.61 nm, back to mg/kg
wl <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(names(forageLIBS)))
line <- forageLIBS[[which.min(abs(wl - 257.61))]]
fit <- robust_boxcox(forageLIBS[1:300, "Mn", drop = FALSE])
model <- lm(Mn ~ log(line), data = data.frame(Mn = fit$transformation$Mn,
                                               line = line[1:300]))
pred <- data.frame(Mn = predict(model, data.frame(line = line[301:368])))
med <- predict(fit, pred, inverse = TRUE)
avg <- predict(fit, pred, inverse = TRUE, estimate = "mean",
               residuals = residuals(model))
summary(avg$Mn / med$Mn)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>   1.039   1.042   1.044   1.045   1.047   1.060 
# the mean content of the 68 samples
c(median = mean(med$Mn), mean = mean(avg$Mn),
  reference = mean(forageLIBS$Mn[301:368]))
#>    median      mean reference 
#>  50.30665  52.65768  57.33824
